segments.say: Our ordinary memory is now in the system, but it's fragile. To understand what turns a fragile trace into something that stays, we need to meet the most studied patient in the history of neuroscience. For more than fifty years, scientists knew him only by two letters, H.M.

His name was Henry Molaison. He was born in 1926, and from his teenage years he suffered from severe epileptic seizures, which grew so bad that ordinary life became very hard. By his twenties, nothing the doctors tried could control them.

In 1953, when Henry was 27, a surgeon named William Scoville decided on a drastic step. In a hospital in Hartford, Connecticut, he removed parts of Henry's brain on both sides, deep in the temporal lobes, including most of a structure called the hippocampus. It was the kind of operation that would never be done today, and it was done in good faith, to stop his seizures.

The seizures did become milder. But something else had changed. Henry could talk, reason, and remember his childhood. His intelligence was normal. But when the conversation moved on, so did he. New events, new faces, new facts, none of them stayed. Each new day was, in a sense, the first.

In 1957, Scoville and a young Canadian psychologist, Brenda Milner, reported his case. They described a profound loss of recent memory after removal of both hippocampi, with otherwise normal intelligence and perception. It was one of the clearest hints that memory is not spread evenly across the brain, and that certain structures have a special job.

show.what: Described the loss of recent memory after removal of the hippocampus on both sides

segments.say: What was lost was mostly the ability to turn new experiences into lasting memories. He could hold a few digits in mind for a short while, so his workspace was fine. And old skills and early memories were largely intact. The part that was broken was the route from the workspace into long-term storage.
Then came the discovery that changed how psychologists think about memory.

show.title: A memory he didn't know he had

segments.say: Brenda Milner asked Henry to trace the outline of a star, while looking at his hand only in a mirror. It's a tricky skill, and most people are clumsy at first. Over several days, Henry got steadily better at it, with fewer mistakes each day. Suzanne Corkin published a detailed account in 1968. But each day, he said he had never done the task before.

show.where: Studies in the 1960s and published in 1968
show.what: Asked H.M. to trace a star while looking only at its reflection in a mirror

segments.say: That was a quiet revolution. It showed that there is more than one kind of memory. One kind is the memory for events and facts, the sort you can say aloud, and that depends on the hippocampus. Another is the memory for skills, which seems to run on different circuitry, and which was working perfectly well in Henry.

If you've ever sat on a bicycle after years and found your balance returned, that's the second kind. You can't tell anyone how you do it. You can't recall the day you learned it. And yet, your body remembers.
So what was the hippocampus doing? The most widely held idea is that it helps new memories settle in, a process called consolidation.

The word comes from a German experiment in 1900. Georg Müller and Alfons Pilzecker asked volunteers to learn a list of nonsense syllables, and then, in some cases, learn a second list straight after. Learning the second list right away hurt memory for the first more than waiting a few minutes did. They suggested that a new memory needs a little time to set.

show.what: Asked people to learn lists of syllables, and varied what happened right afterwards

segments.say: A useful picture is wet concrete. At first it holds a print easily, and it is easily smudged. After a while it hardens, and a print stays. In the same way, a new memory seems to be soft at first, easily disturbed by other things, and gradually firmer.

In the most common version of this idea, associated with Larry Squire and others, the hippocampus acts like a quick learner that binds the pieces of an experience together. Over time, those links are slowly built into the wider network of the cortex, and the memory depends less and less on the hippocampus.

show.title: What consolidation seems to mean
items: The hippocampus helps bind the pieces
Over time, the memory leans less on it
Older memories live more in the cortex

segments.say: It also fits an observation from 1881, by the French psychologist Théodule Ribot. In many kinds of amnesia, the most recent memories are lost first, and old ones are spared. And Henry's case fit. He had lost the years just before his surgery too, though his early life was still there.

There is something quietly hopeful in that. It suggests that the first hours and nights are a sort of sensitive period, when a new memory is still being built. And what you do with that time, including how you sleep, might matter.

Henry Molaison died in 2008, and arrangements had been made so that his brain could be studied. In 2009, a team in San Diego, led by Jacopo Annese, cut it into more than two thousand extremely thin slices, and photographed each one. The resulting digital atlas, published in 2014, is still used by researchers.

When the world learned his name, people learned a good deal about him too. Those who knew him described a gentle, patient man with a sense of humour, who was always willing to help the scientists, because he understood that his experience might help others.

Henry's story shows how much we depend on the hippocampus. But there is a hopeful second half to the story, because that part of the brain doesn't seem to be fixed. It seems to respond to what we ask of it.

show.title: A hippocampus that changes with use

segments.say: In 2000, Eleanor Maguire and colleagues scanned the brains of licensed London taxi drivers. To earn a licence, a driver must learn thousands of streets, a challenge known as the Knowledge, which takes years. The back portion of the taxi drivers' hippocampus was larger than in other people, and it was larger the longer they had been driving.

show.what: Scanned the brains of London taxi drivers who had memorised the city's streets

segments.say: You might reasonably wonder whether people with large hippocampi simply become taxi drivers. A later study answered that. In 2011, Katherine Woollett and Eleanor Maguire followed trainee drivers for several years. Those who passed the exam showed growth in that part of the brain. Those who failed did not.

That doesn't mean that anyone can grow a bigger memory by effort alone, and the changes were small. It suggests that the hippocampus responds to experience, especially to learning a rich map. And the same part of the brain that helps you find your way across a city also helps you find your way back into your own past.
Many of us picture amnesia from films. A knock on the head, a hospital bed, and a person who wakes up unable to remember who they are. It makes a good story. How close is it?

In 2004, the neuropsychologist Sallie Baxendale reviewed dozens of films that feature amnesia, and compared them with real patients. In films, the most common story is a person who forgets their own identity after a blow to the head, and then recovers it with another blow. In real life, that pattern is extremely rare.

show.what: Reviewed how amnesia is shown in films, and compared it with real cases

segments.say: The most common real form is the one we saw with Henry, which is difficulty forming new memories, while the sense of who you are stays largely intact. People rarely forget their own name. And a second knock on the head does not usually bring it all back. Real amnesia is quieter, and in many ways more poignant, than the movie version.

So here is what one man's story taught us. Memory depends on special brain structures. The workspace and the long-term store are separate. There is more than one kind of memory. And new memories need time to settle.

show.title: What Henry taught us
items: Memory depends on special brain structures
The workspace and long-term storage are separate
There is more than one kind of memory
New memories need time to settle

segments.say: And that raises a lovely question for the hours when you aren't doing anything at all. If a new memory needs time and quiet to settle, what is your brain doing while you sleep? The answer might be one of the loveliest findings in this whole subject.
